content: Chlorpromazine is a typical antipsychotic drug classified as an aliphatic phenothiazine. It is one of the most extensively studied first-generation antipsychotic medications and has been used as a benchmark to evaluate the efficacy of both older and newer antipsychotic drugs. Despite the widespread promotion of newer, more expensive antipsychotic medications as superior treatments for schizophrenia, this claim may not always hold true and could lead to unnecessary financial strain on limited healthcare resources. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of chlorpromazine with those of atypical or second-generation antipsychotic drugs in the treatment of schizophrenia. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared chlorpromazine with other atypical antipsychotics in adults diagnosed with schizophrenia or related disorders, such as schizophreniform, schizoaffective, and delusional disorders. Data were extracted and analyzed independently by at least two reviewers, with risk ratios (RR) and mean differences (MD) calculated for dichotomous and continuous data, respectively. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Chlorpromazine versus Olanzapine In the short term, individuals treated with olanzapine demonstrated a significantly greater clinical response compared to those receiving chlorpromazine (3 RCTs, 204 participants; RR 2.34, 95% CI 1.37 to 3.99; low-quality evidence). However, there was no significant difference between the two drugs in terms of relapse rates (1 RCT, 70 participants; RR 1.5, 95% CI 0.46 to 4.86; very low-quality evidence) or mental state as measured by the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) (4 RCTs, 245 participants; MD 3.21, 95% CI −0.62 to 7.05; very low-quality evidence). Patients receiving chlorpromazine experienced significantly more extrapyramidal symptoms compared to those on olanzapine (2 RCTs, 298 participants; RR 34.47, 95% CI 4.79 to 248.30; very low-quality evidence). Quality of life, as assessed by the physical health subscale of the General Quality of Life Interview (GQOLI), was more favorable in the olanzapine group (1 RCT, 61 participants; MD −10.10, 95% CI −13.93 to −6.27; very low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference in the rate of study discontinuation between the two groups (3 RCTs, 139 participants; RR 1.69, 95% CI 0.45 to 6.40; very low-quality evidence). Chlorpromazine versus Risperidone In the short term, there was no significant difference in clinical response between chlorpromazine and risperidone (7 RCTs, 475 participants; RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.34; low-quality evidence). Similarly, no significant differences were observed in mental state as measured by the BPRS (4 RCTs, 247 participants; MD 0.90, 95% CI −3.49 to 5.28; very low-quality evidence) or in the occurrence of extrapyramidal adverse effects (3 RCTs, 235 participants; RR 1.7, 95% CI 0.85 to 3.40; very low-quality evidence). Quality of life, as measured by the QOL scale, was significantly better in the risperidone group (1 RCT, 100 participants; MD −14.2, 95% CI −20.50 to −7.90; very low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference in the rate of study discontinuation between the two groups (1 RCT, 41 participants; RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.11; very low-quality evidence). Chlorpromazine versus Quetiapine In the short term, there was no significant difference in clinical response between chlorpromazine and quetiapine (28 RCTs, 3241 participants; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.06; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, no significant differences were observed in mental state as measured by the BPRS (6 RCTs, 548 participants; MD −0.18, 95% CI −1.23 to 0.88; very low-quality evidence). Quality of life, as assessed by the GQOL1-74 scale, was significantly better in the quetiapine group (1 RCT, 59 participants; MD −6.49, 95% CI −11.30 to −1.68; very low-quality evidence). Patients receiving chlorpromazine experienced significantly more extrapyramidal adverse effects compared to those on quetiapine (8 RCTs, 644 participants; RR 8.03, 95% CI 4.78 to 13.51; low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference in the rate of study discontinuation between the two groups in the short term (12 RCTs, 1223 participants; RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.41; moderate-quality evidence). Authors' Conclusions The majority of the included trials were conducted in hospital settings in China, making the findings more applicable to the Chinese population. Most studies were short-term, limiting the ability to draw conclusions about the mediumand long-term use of chlorpromazine compared to atypical antipsychotics. Low-quality evidence suggests that chlorpromazine is associated with a higher incidence of extrapyramidal adverse effects. However, the included studies used varying dose ranges, and higher doses of chlorpromazine are expected to result in more adverse events.
